title: Cell 5 (center) in the Sobel Gx kernel
t: Cell 5 (center) in the Sobel Gx kernel
description: The center cell of Sobel Gx: value 0, which neighbor it weights, and its measured share of the edge response.
cell_role: Cell 5 (center) of the 3x3 kernel grid weights the pixel the pixel being processed itself. Sobel Gx 0, Sobel Gy 0; Prewitt Gx 0, Prewitt Gy 0; Scharr Gx 0, Scharr Gy 0. It is silent in both Sobel gradient estimates -- the pivot cell.
demo_code:
# Nine-number kernel lab -- pure-Python 3x3 convolution, zero dependencies.
# Images are 2-D brightness lists; the demo convolves the interior 3x3.
SOBEL_GX = [[-1,0,1],[-2,0,2],[-1,0,1]]
SOBEL_GY = [[-1,-2,-1],[0,0,0],[1,2,1]]
PREWITT_GX = [[-1,0,1],[-1,0,1],[-1,0,1]]
PREWITT_GY = [[-1,-1,-1],[0,0,0],[1,1,1]]
SCHARR_GX = [[-3,0,3],[-10,0,10],[-3,0,3]]
SCHARR_GY = [[-3,-10,-3],[0,0,0],[3,10,3]]
V = [[10,10,10,200,200] for _ in range(5)]   # vertical step edge: dark left, bright right
H = [[10]*5,[10]*5,[10]*5,[200]*5,[200]*5]   # horizontal step edge: dark top, bright bottom
F = [[50]*5 for _ in range(5)]               # flat field: no edges at all
D = [[10,10,10,10,10],[10,10,10,10,200],[10,10,10,200,200],[10,10,200,200,200],[10,200,200,200,200]]  # diagonal edge
def conv(img, k):
    return [[sum(img[y+dy-1][x+dx-1]*k[dy][dx] for dy in range(3) for dx in range(3))
             for x in range(1,4)] for y in range(1,4)]
def show(m):
    for row in m:
        print(" ".join("%8g" % v for v in row))
r, c = 1, 1
k = SOBEL_GX
out = conv(V, k)
print("Sobel Gx convolved over the vertical step edge (interior 3x3 output):")
show(out)
touch = V[1+r][1+c]
contrib = touch * k[r][c]
print("cell value:", k[r][c], "| brightness of the pixel it weights:", touch)
print("this cell contribution at output (2,2):", contrib, "of total", out[1][1])
print("share of edge signal: %.1f %%" % (100.0*contrib/out[1][1]))

       0      760      760
cell value: 0 | brightness of the pixel it weights: 10

share of edge signal: 0.0 %
body:
Cell 5 sits at the center of the 3-by-3 Sobel Gx kernel, and its value is 0. The Gx kernel estimates the horizontal brightness gradient -- how fast the image gets brighter or darker moving left to right -- while smoothing vertically to calm noise. This cell weights the pixel the pixel being processed itself: whatever brightness that neighbor holds is multiplied by 0 and added into the gradient estimate. Because the value is zero, this position is silent: it contributes nothing, and the kernel's differencing column stays perfectly balanced. As the center cell it is the pivot the whole operator turns on -- and every one of the three operators sets it to 0.

The executed demo below convolves the full Sobel Gx kernel over a synthetic vertical step edge (dark 10 on the left, bright 200 on the right) and isolates exactly what this single cell contributes at the edge pixel: 0 out of a total response of 760 (0.0 percent of the edge signal comes through this one cell).

body:
In the Prewitt operator (1970) the center cell (cell 5) holds 0 in Gx and 0 in Gy. Prewitt is Sobel's plainer sibling: where Sobel doubles the middle row's smoothing weight to 2, Prewitt trusts every row equally with weight 1, so its kernels are uniform. That makes Prewitt simpler and cheaper, but a little more nervous around noise -- the center row gets no extra vote. As the center cell it is the pivot the whole operator turns on -- and every one of the three operators sets it to 0.

The executed demo runs both Prewitt kernels over the step edges. In Gx this cell contributes 0 out of a total 570; in Gy it contributes 0 out of 570. Compare with Sobel's 760: Prewitt's edge answer is weaker by exactly the smoothing-weight ratio, because every Prewitt row carries weight 1 where Sobel's middle row carries 2.

In the Scharr operator (2000) the center cell (cell 5) holds 0 in Gx and 0 in Gy. Scharr kept Sobel's shape but re-optimized the numbers for rotational symmetry: its gradient direction estimates stay truer as an edge rotates, which is why libraries reach for Scharr when the angle of the edge matters, not just its strength. The price is louder numbers -- 3 and 10 where Sobel uses 1 and 2 -- so Scharr's raw responses run about four times hotter. As the center cell it is the pivot the whole operator turns on -- and every one of the three operators sets it to 0.

body:
Cell 5 (center) does not treat every edge orientation equally. Gx is the vertical-edge finder (it reacts when brightness changes left to right) and Gy is the horizontal-edge finder (it reacts when brightness changes top to bottom). A cell with a nonzero Gx weight takes part in finding vertical edges; a cell with a nonzero Gy weight takes part in finding horizontal ones. Measured at the edge pixel, this cell contributes Gx-on-vertical-edge 0, Gy-on-vertical-edge 0, Gx-on-horizontal-edge 0, and Gy-on-horizontal-edge 0. In plain terms: it is blind to vertical edges and it is blind to horizontal edges.

The executed demo prints exactly that four-way table for this cell. Notice the pattern across the grid: the middle column (cells 2, 5, 8) carries Gx weight 0, so it never helps find vertical edges, and the middle row (cells 4, 5, 6) carries Gy weight 0, so it never helps find horizontal edges. Only the four corner cells work both jobs -- one reason corners matter more than their size suggests.

body:
What happens if cell 5 (center) is not 0? The sensitivity experiment varies just this one cell of Sobel Gx through -2, -1, 0, 1, 2 and measures two things at the edge pixel: the response on the vertical step edge, and the response on a perfectly flat field (brightness 50 everywhere, no edge at all).

Two real, measured facts come out. First, the edge response moves linearly with the cell: every +1 added to the cell shifts the edge answer by 10, the brightness of the pixel this cell weights -- the cell's influence is exactly its weight times its pixel, no more, no less. Second, touching the cell breaks the kernel's zero-sum balance: on the flat field, where the true answer is 0, the response becomes 50 times the cell's deviation from its designed value. A single changed cell makes empty sky report edges. That is why kernel design is conservative: the numbers are a balanced set, and each one earns its place by keeping flat regions quiet while letting real edges shout. The executed demo prints the full variation table.

PREWITT_GX = [[-1,0,1],[-1,0,1],[-1,0,1]]
PREWITT_GY = [[-1,-1,-1],[0,0,0],[1,1,1]]
SCHARR_GX = [[-3,0,3],[-10,0,10],[-3,0,3]]
SCHARR_GY = [[-3,-10,-3],[0,0,0],[3,10,3]]
V = [[10,10,10,200,200] for _ in range(5)]   # vertical step edge: dark left, bright right

    return [[sum(img[y+dy-1][x+dx-1]*k[dy][dx] for dy in range(3) for dx in range(3))
             for x in range(1,4)] for y in range(1,4)]
def show(m):
    for row in m:
        print(" ".join("%8g" % v for v in row))
SMOOTH = {'sobel':[1,2,1],'prewitt':[1,1,1],'scharr':[3,10,3]}
DIFF = [-1,0,1]
def outer(s,d):
    return [[s[i]*d[j] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)]
print("Sobel Gx == smooth[1,2,1] x diff[-1,0,1]:", outer(SMOOTH["sobel"],DIFF)==SOBEL_GX)
print("Prewitt Gx == smooth[1,1,1] x diff[-1,0,1]:", outer(SMOOTH["prewitt"],DIFF)==PREWITT_GX)
print("Scharr Gx == smooth[3,10,3] x diff[-1,0,1]:", outer(SMOOTH["scharr"],DIFF)==SCHARR_GX)
r, c = 1, 1
for name in ['sobel','prewitt','scharr']:
    s, d = SMOOTH[name][r], DIFF[c]
    print("cell 5 in %s Gx = smooth[%d] x diff[%d] = %d x %d = %d" % (name, r, c, s, d, s*d))
print("Gy transposed: cell = diff[row] x smooth[col]:")
for name, k in [('sobel',SOBEL_GY),('prewitt',PREWITT_GY),('scharr',SCHARR_GY)]:
    print("cell 5 in %s Gy = %d x %d = %d" % (name, DIFF[r], SMOOTH[name][c], k[r][c]))

body:
Every one of these 3x3 kernels is secretly two 1-D filters multiplied together: a smoothing filter down the rows times a differencing filter across the columns. That is why cell 5 (center) always factors as smoothing[1] x differencing[1]: sobel 2x0=0; prewitt 1x0=0; scharr 10x0=0. For Gy the idea is transposed: the cell is differencing[row] x smoothing[column].

This factorization is the famous 'trust' interpretation: the smoothing number is somebody's opinion about how much you ought to trust the row of pixels you happen to be standing on. Sobel says the middle row deserves double trust (2); Prewitt says trust every row equally (1); Scharr says the middle row deserves the most trust of all (10, with 3 for the outer rows). Cell 5's own values across the three operators are just that opinion, multiplied by the differencing sign of its column. The executed demo verifies the outer-product decomposition numerically for all three Gx kernels and prints this cell's factorization in each.

Cell 5 (center), all six values side by side: sobel_gx=0, sobel_gy=0, prewitt_gx=0, prewitt_gy=0, scharr_gx=0, scharr_gy=0. The operator that leans on this position hardest is Sobel Gx with magnitude 0. On the standard vertical step edge the three Gx kernels answer 760 (Sobel), 570 (Prewitt), 3040 (Scharr) -- the 4:3:16 ratio of their positive-side weight sums (Sobel 1+2+1=4, Prewitt 1+1+1=3, Scharr 3+10+3=16), measured live, not assumed.

A note on the famous middle number: the popular telling says 'the middle number is 2' for Sobel, 1 for Prewitt, 10 for Scharr -- but that number lives in the middle ROW (cells 4 and 6), the vertical trust weights, not in this center cell. The center itself is 0 in all six kernels: the pivot the whole operator turns on, the one value all three operators agree must stay silent.
